newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia retail data leaves questions over rates.
newsitem.headline: Australia retail data leaves questions over rates.

text.p: Australian financial markets, anticipating another interest rate cut at any time, were left without a clear indication about the economy's direction on Wednesday, despite a firm rise in May retail sales.
Economists said financial markets, expecting another rate cut as early as this morning, had looked to new retail data to provide a clear statement on the health of the economy.
But this had failed to materialise, they said.
"Unfortunately, I don't think it (retail trade) really gives us the definitive answer we have been looking for," Commonwealth Bank of Australia Ltd senior economist Michael Blythe told Reuters.
Economists said although the strength of the 2.9 percent rise in May retail sales was surprising, it still only partially offset the weakness of the previous two months.
It did little to change expectations of another interest rate cut, they said.
The 2.9 percent jump was retail trade's highest rise since March 1994. The increase followed a 1.7 percent fall in April and a 0.3 percent drop in March.
Forecasts had centred on a 2.0 percent rise and ranged from a 0.2 percent fall to a rise of 3.0 percent.

"Retail spending is only travelling along at a very moderate pace and is certainly not strong enough at this stage to preclude another rate reduction by the RBA (Reserve Bank of Australia)," said J.P. Morgan senior economist John Kyriakopoulos.
Other figures out on Wednesday showed building approvals rose 2.2 percent in May, but economists remained unconvinced that either set of numbers spelt any huge economic change.
"Activity still remains fairly modest and we do expect a further easing in interest rates," Colonial State Bank senior economist Craig James said.
The RBA last eased monetary policy on May 23, cutting official cash rates by 50 basis points to 5.5 percent.
It was the fourth equal rate cut in less than a year.
The data met with a mixed reaction from the markets with the credit market factoring in another rate cut, while the Australian dollar reacted to expectations that rate cut chances had eased.
The 10-year bond future was at 93.000, unchanged on the day after being as high as 93.070 and as low as 92.915.
The Australian dollar rose to US$0.7533/38 after the release of the figures, up from US$0.7510/15 at the opening.
